issues.item: Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Night' implies fear linked to darkness/outdoor danger, but there are no Threat items and no memory/trigger content tied to night-time, darkness, or outdoor contexts. For this relief-worker trauma, that strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the least coherent item because it addresses a threat context not otherwise represented across Triggers, Memory, or Negative Appraisals.

This creates a contradiction with the formulation structure, especially given concurrent trigger and memory items that imply exactly the kind of reminder-linked threat activation the model marks as inactive. The other nodes are broadly coherent with each other and with the trauma type.

Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time' overlaps almost exactly with Threat: 'Scanning for Danger' and Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings,' which contradicts the formulation because Threat has no active links to or from these nodes.

Threat: 'Negative Emotions' is very broad and non-specific, while the rest of the profile centers on intrusive reliving, moral/entrapment triggers, and vigilance-based coping; as a Threat item it does not fit the otherwise isolated, weakly integrated role of threat in this formulation.

vignette: Mr. Lin, an 80-year-old widowed data scientist of South Eastern Asian descent, sought help after a lifetime of service in war zones began to take its psychological toll. His experiences as a relief worker in the chaos and violence of conflict zones have left him haunted by memories that refuse to fade into the past. Mr. Lin's most potent triggers are moral violations-people misbehaving-and feelings of entrapment, particularly when he feels there are no options. These triggers often arise from news reports about similar events, which Mr. Lin now avoids at all costs. The mere mention of war or conflict sends a cascade of negative emotions through him, leaving him feeling like his body is constantly on high alert, ready to react to any perceived danger. Mr. Lin's fear that his reactions mean he is "going crazy" has only compounded these symptoms. He frequently wakes up from nightmares, reliving the terrifying events as if they were happening in real-time. These dreams are often followed by intense irritability and outbursts of anger, which further reinforce his belief that he cannot control his emotions. The experience of moral violation triggers Mr. Lin's maladaptive strategies, such as rehearsing conversations before any interaction to avoid saying the wrong thing. He also constantly checks his surroundings for signs of threat, a behavior that has grown increasingly prominent in recent months. This hyper-vigilance often leads him back into memories of past traumas, where he relives the frightening events over and over again. Mr. Lin's belief that the world is inherently dangerous fuels both his maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals. He feels that every situation might spiral out of control at any moment, which keeps him in a constant state of fear and anger. This fear is exacerbated by the memory replay of traumatic events, where the line between past and present blurs. Mr. Lin's work as a data scientist has been deeply affected by these triggers. His need to avoid news reports means that he often misses important updates related to his field, which can be critical in the fast-paced world of technology. This avoidance has strained his relationships with colleagues who rely on him for timely information and insights. The cycle of Mr. Lin's symptoms has tightened over time. When he feels entrapment or sees moral violations, it triggers a flood of negative emotions and memories that replay incessantly. These memories, in turn, lead to hyper-vigilance and avoidance behaviors, which only deepen his sense of fear and loss of control. Mr. Lin's most significant hope is to regain some sense of normalcy and feel safe again. He recognizes that the triggers are overwhelming him but is also terrified that he might do something terrible if he cannot manage his emotions better. The combination of these fears and hopes brought him to seek help, hoping to break this cycle before it consumes him entirely. Mr. Lin's current state is one of increasing anxiety and irritability, with a growing sense of isolation as the world around him seems more dangerous every day. He has come to believe that only through understanding and managing his triggers can he regain control over his life and feel safe once again.
